entries.clue: Verse collection: Dante’s Inferno at beginning, trying to grapple with evil and ending in Paradiso? (6,7)

indicatorNotes.at beginning: Asks for each of the two words only at its beginning, its opening letter.
indicatorNotes.grapple: Things that grapple are twisted and tangled together, so the letters caught up in it are thrown out of order.

blocks.note: the opening letters of Dante’s and Inferno

blocks.clueFragment: trying to grapple with evil and ending in Paradiso
blocks.note: TRYING and EVIL plus O, the last letter of Paradiso, jumbled

annotation.surface: A reader struggling through Dante's great poem, from the horrors of Hell to its final heavenly book.
annotation.walkthrough: Inferno and Paradiso look like titles to admire, but they only donate letters; the question mark admits Dante's poem is really called a comedy, though it does come in three parts.
annotation.definitionFit: A trilogy is a set of three works, and one of divine subject in verse is a collection of poems.

entries.clue: Blood count? (7)

annotation.surface: A nurse asking for the result of a blood test.
annotation.walkthrough: A blood count is a routine lab test; read as a nobleman with a taste for blood, the Count is Bram Stoker's vampire.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a pun: Count is Dracula's title, and blood is what the vampire feeds on.

blocks.note: what the surface pushes: a lab test tallying cells in a blood sample
what the setter means: a nobleman, the Count, who is all about blood

entries.clue: Victor, denied entrance, opens wide and inhales a cloud of nicotine (5)

indicatorNotes.denied entrance: The entrance of a word is its first letter; denying it takes that letter away, and Victor fills the gap.

blocks.note: V is Victor in the phonetic alphabet
GAPES without its first letter G

annotation.surface: A man called Victor, turned away at the door, stands outside gaping and puffing on an e-cigarette.
annotation.walkthrough: Victor looks like a person's name; it is the radio code for V, which takes the place of the G of GAPES.
annotation.definitionFit: To vape is to breathe in nicotine vapour from an electronic cigarette.

entries.clue: More likely to inquire about one that’s less quiet (7)

blocks.note: someone nosier pries more

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether the one making more noise is also the more inquisitive.
annotation.walkthrough: About looks like it means concerning; here it wraps NOSIER around I.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain comparative synonym: making more noise is the same as being less quiet.

entries.clue: You get at least 66 points playing a quiz here (6-4,5)

annotation.definition: You get at least 66 points playing a quiz here
annotation.surface: A pub quiz where a good team can rack up plenty of points.
annotation.walkthrough: The quiz is not a trivia night: in Scrabble the tiles of QUIZ and A are worth 23, and laid on a triple-word square that becomes 69.
annotation.definitionFit: A triple-word score is the Scrabble square that trebles the value of the word played across it.

blocks.clueFragment: You get at least 66 points playing a quiz
blocks.note: what the surface pushes: a team scoring well at a quiz night
what the setter means: laying the tiles A, Q, U, I, Z on a Scrabble board, worth 23 before the square trebles them

entries.clue: Yorkshireman’s ultimately mean (6)

indicatorNotes.Yorkshireman’s: Said the Yorkshire way, 'the' is clipped to a bare t', so the HE of THE is dropped.

blocks.note: a three-word phrase meaning finally

annotation.surface: A blunt Yorkshireman who, in the end, turns out to be stingy.
annotation.walkthrough: Mean wants to be the Yorkshire stereotype of tight-fistedness; it is the verb. Yorkshire dialect shortens the to t', so 'in the end' becomes 'in t' end'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym when followed by a verb: to mean to go and to intend to go are the same thing.

entries.clue: Reconsidered when decapitated, would roses suggest this description? (9)

annotation.definition: Reconsidered when decapitated, would roses suggest this description?

indicatorNotes.Reconsidered: What is reconsidered is thought through again and rearranged, so the letters are put in a new order.
indicatorNotes.decapitated: Decapitating removes the head, the first letter W.

blocks.note: WOULD ROSES without its head W, then rearranged

annotation.surface: A wry question: would anyone looking at a rose really call it scentless?
annotation.walkthrough: The expected answer to the question is no, since roses are famous for their scent; that tease is the whole clue's reading, while its middle words are also the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Odourless means having no smell, a description nobody would apply to roses.

entries.clue: Flipping Everyman’s installing malfunctioning radar as onboard support (7)

indicatorNotes.Flipping: Flipping something turns it over, so MY comes out backwards as YM.
indicatorNotes.installing: To install something is to put it inside, so YM holds the other letters.
indicatorNotes.malfunctioning: A radar that is malfunctioning is not working properly, so its letters are out of order.

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, speaking of what is his
RADAR rearranged

annotation.surface: An angry setter complaining that a broken radar has been fitted on his ship.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman's stands for the setter's own MY; flipped to YM, it takes in the scrambled RADAR.
annotation.definitionFit: A yardarm is the end of a spar that supports a sail on a ship.

annotation.surface: A slug crawling towards a light.
annotation.walkthrough: Slug looks like the garden creature; it is the verb to punch, and lamp is slang for hitting someone hard.
annotation.definitionFit: To lamp someone is to hit them, and a lamp gives light.

blocks.note: slug as a verb, to punch hard; British slang has a matching four-letter verb
something that gives out light

entries.clue: A laundry refitted in approx. 709 hours (5,3)

indicatorNotes.refitted: What is refitted is put together again differently, so the letters are rebuilt in a new order.

blocks.note: the fodder

annotation.surface: A laundrette being refurbished, with the work taking about a month.
annotation.walkthrough: The oddly exact figure is the definition: a lunar day, from one sunrise on the Moon to the next, lasts about 29.5 Earth days.
annotation.definitionFit: A lunar day lasts about 29.5 days, which is about 709 hours.

entries.clue: The old ready for 3d info stored digitally? (10,3)

blocks.note: d was the symbol for a penny in old British money
a bit is the smallest unit of digital data

annotation.surface: Old technology ready to handle three-dimensional digital files.
annotation.walkthrough: 3d looks like three-dimensional; in pre-1971 British money d meant pennies. The ready is slang for cash, and the threepenny bit was a coin worth 3d.
annotation.definitionFit: The threepenny bit was a coin of old British money, and the ready means cash.
